The request scheduler below is intentionally ordinary text rather than a benchmark
prompt. It is used as a fixed token stream for teacher-forced speculative decoding
diagnostics, so the content should remain stable unless the fixture version changes.

At startup, the controller loads the model registry, validates that every declared
endpoint has a matching health check, and writes a small readiness record to the
state directory. Each worker then accepts a shard of requests, sorts the shard by
arrival time, and keeps the original request id attached to every row. When a
request enters prefill, the worker records the prompt length, the cache slot, and
the first sampling configuration observed by the OpenAI-compatible server.

During decode, the worker advances exactly one target step at a time. The target
model produces the next-token argmax, while the draft model proposes a short chain
of speculative tokens from the same prefix. The verifier compares token ids, not
decoded strings, because whitespace and punctuation can have multiple surface
forms. Accepted tokens are appended to the running sequence, rejected tokens are
discarded, and the next target token starts a fresh speculative event. Metrics are
reported as per-position acceptance rates so a root failure cannot be hidden by
later full-chain matches.

The diagnostic mode in this fixture removes generated-text divergence. Instead of
letting either server choose the next prefix, the client feeds both servers the
same reference token sequence. For each prefix, the client asks for one greedy
token and records two values: the draft model's top-one chain and the target
model's argmax token. If the tree server matches the standalone server under this
forced sequence, then any previous per-position gap came from the two systems
continuing different text. If the draft chain differs while the target argmax
matches, the proposer is wrong. If the target argmax differs, the target forward
path is not equivalent and the tree path needs deeper attention-state debugging.
